title: The King's Pawn Openings
summary: Every reply to 1.e4 is a different bargain

steps.title: Two Lines in One Push
steps.text:
One pawn move frees two pieces. Push the e-pawn and the queen and the light-squared bishop both get a road out of the back rank.

So these games fill up early. Pieces arrive, lines open, and the armies are touching while both kings are still standing in the middle. A slow move costs more here than it does in a quiet position, because somebody is already out there to punish it.

steps.title: The Pawn With No Guard
steps.text:
Black copied, and copying has a price: the second player has to answer a question that was already asked.

The knight on f3 attacks the pawn on e5. Count the defenders of e5 and you get none.

There are two honest ways to fix that. A piece can guard the pawn and leave home in the same move, spending nothing. A pawn can guard it just as well, and pay for the job by standing in front of one of Black's own bishops for the rest of the game.

steps.prompt: Guard the pawn White's knight has just attacked, and hold your share of the middle.
steps.hint: One defender is a piece that wanted to come out anyway; the other is a pawn that pays a bishop for the work. Either is a main line.

steps.title: The Oldest Argument
steps.text:
Guard e5 with the knight and White has a move waiting. {{Bb5}} ignores the pawn on e5 entirely and goes after the piece defending it: take away the guard and the pawn is loose.

Black shoves the bishop with {{a6}}, the bishop slides back down the diagonal with {{Ba4}}, still aiming at the same knight and still costing nothing. That is the Ruy Lopez, four centuries old and still the most argued-over opening there is.

steps.title: Three Ways to Refuse
steps.text:
Most strong replies to the king's pawn never touch e5 at all. Each refuses in a different currency.

- **The Sicilian** leaves e4 alone and fights for d4 with a pawn to c5, taking the half-open c-file when the pawns trade there.
- **The Caro-Kann** and **the French** spend a quiet move on c6 or e6 first, so the push to d5 arrives with backup — the French shuts its light-squared bishop in behind the wall, the Caro-Kann keeps it out.
- **Alekhine's Defense** sends a knight to f6 and dares White's pawns to chase it.

steps.title: A Refusal in Progress
steps.text:
Black spent move one on a pawn to c6, and White took everything on offer: two pawns abreast on d4 and e4, the widest center White ever gets for free.

Wide is not safe. A big pawn center has to be met while it is still only pawns — leave it alone and White's pieces come out behind it and the whole wall rolls forward.

Move one was not modesty. It was a pawn stationed to back up a strike that has not happened yet.

> A quiet first move is a loud second move waiting its turn.

steps.prompt: Meet White's two-pawn center with the pawn that your quiet first move was posted to support.
steps.hint: Move one was a pawn with a single job. Ask which square it covers, and notice that nobody has occupied that square yet.
